title: A handful of leaves
hook: the Buddha holds a few leaves: what I have taught is this; what I know is the forest; I taught what helps (SN 56.31)

segments.voice: Yesterday: three turns, and your line, three turns. Did you notice which turn you were on with one thing: knowing it, knowing what to do, or having done it? Day three hundred forty-five.

A cook copies out a family recipe on the back of an envelope: five ingredients, three steps. She knows far more than that. The history of the dish, why the onions go in first, the aunt who taught her. She leaves it out on purpose, because the friend holding the envelope needs to make dinner tonight. The handful of leaves came up briefly on the last day of year one, as a lookout over the road ahead. Today it comes back in its home, the book of the Connected Discourses on the four truths, and this time we'll read it slowly: the setting, the full list of reasons, and the test it leaves behind.
screen: `A RECIPE ON AN ENVELOPE.` → `SHE LEAVES THE REST OUT.` → `READ IT SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees near Kosambi. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, these in my hand or the leaves in the grove overhead? The leaves in the grove, they say, by far. In the same way, he says, the things I have directly known but not taught are far more. Then comes the part that's easy to skip. Why hasn't he taught them? Because, he says, they aren't beneficial. They don't belong to the basics of the holy life. They don't lead to letting go, to calm, to peace, to direct knowing, to awakening, to nibbana. And what has he taught? This is dukkha. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Why? Because that does help. It leads to letting go, to calm, to peace, to awakening. So the handful isn't a random sample. It's a careful choice, and the filter is simple: does it help? Notice that the Buddha isn't hiding anything mysterious behind his back, or saying the rest of the forest is forbidden. He's being a teacher who knows what a student needs, the way the cook knows her friend needs dinner. Fittingly, this sutta sits in the book of the four truths. It's the Buddha explaining why the last two weeks have been about four sentences and not four hundred. And it hands us a test we can use on anything we read, watch, or worry about: does this lead to calm and freedom, or just to more noise?
screen: `WHICH ARE MORE?` · `WHY NOT THE FOREST?` · `WHAT'S IN THE HAND.` · `THE FILTER: DOES IT HELP?` · then, large: `ONLY WHAT HELPS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold a handful of leaves. If you can, pick up a few real leaves from outside, or anything small: a few coins, some dried beans. Hold them loosely in your open palm. Feel their weight, and how little it is. Then, breathing slowly, let your mind fill with everything you're carrying today: plans, news, worries. For each one, ask quietly: is this in the handful, or is it the forest? Let the forest go. The bell holds the time.
A handful of leaves. What the Buddha taught, compared to what he knew: a small handful, chosen because it helps toward peace and freedom.
Your line: only what helps. Today, before you open one more tab or start one more worry, ask the Buddha's question: does this help? If not, leave it in the forest. Day three hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often tell the story of the simsapa leaves to explain why the teaching centers on the four noble truths and on what leads to peace, rather than on every question that can be asked.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the simsapa sutta.
pairs: what he knew but didn't teach
does it lead to peace and awakening?

myth: the Buddha said the leaves in the forest were secret teachings
he left them out because they don't help toward letting go, peace and awakening.
the handful the Buddha taught is the four noble truths
dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way.
the story takes place in a simsapa grove near Kosambi
that's the setting the sutta gives.

fork.setup: you're a monk in the simsapa grove. the Buddha says he knows far more than he's taught. why, he asks, hasn't he taught it?
options: because you aren't ready for secrets.
because it doesn't help toward peace and awakening.
fork.reveal: he says the rest isn't beneficial and doesn't lead to letting go, calm, peace and nibbana; the four truths do.

original.note: Pali siṃsapā: the simsapa tree (often identified as Indian rosewood), whose grove gives the sutta its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: the handful of leaves means the Buddha kept secrets.
what it means: he chose to teach only what helps toward freedom, and named it: the four truths.

what a scholar hears: SN 56.31 sits in the Saccasaṃyutta, the connected sayings on the truths; its list, nibbidā, virāga, nirodha, upasama, abhiññā, sambodhi, nibbāna, recurs in other suttas as the test of what is worth teaching.

sources.ref: SN 56.31 (Simsapa Sutta, the handful of leaves)

notes: This story was told briefly on day 331 (year one close); today's script deliberately focuses on the reasons given in the sutta. Keeper may judge whether the repetition is acceptable.

SN 56.31 paraphrased: confirm the reasons list (not beneficial, not the fundamentals of the holy life, not leading to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, awakening, nibbāna).
Siṃsapā identified as Indian rosewood (Dalbergia sissoo) by many, though some suggest Ashoka tree; the note says 'often identified'. Confirm.
